**Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We thank the reviewer for reading the paper, its appendices and our rebuttal so closely. We believe it takes a great deal of time and effort to arrive at that feedback. We apologise for the slight delay: we wanted the requested control finished first. On the first we stand corrected; on the second we report every cell below.

**1. Which claim is correct: the paper's.**

The paper's claim is correct and holds throughout: §4.1, Table N.2's caption and Appendix H agree. One sentence in our W3 answer described what normalization does to its input, but phrased it as a claim about the encoder's representation. We withdraw it, and want to give visibility into how we got there. Our initial reasoning was that raw input helps Moirai's router for the reason it does on MOMENT, where RevIN removes the statistics and raw routing restores them. That reasoning does not transfer.

Only that clause fails. The diagnosis predicts collapse wherever routing-relevant statistics are stripped from what the router reads. Moirai's routing stays healthy, so those statistics do reach its router, and the gain has the source Table N.2's caption (Moirai-MoE) states: raw-signal routing is information-richer than hidden-state routing even when the hidden states retain enough signal to avoid collapse. The two regimes are therefore collapse-repair where the statistics are stripped, and a richer router input where they are not. This is not App. P.3's Pure Raw-MLP effect: in RR-MoA the raw signal reaches only the router, and the 12–29% figure is RR-MoA against best fixed (Table N.1).

The rule we gave Reviewer 8b2Z is shorthand for the paper's criterion, stated in Appendix H: whether normalization triggers or prevents collapse depends on whether the stripped statistics overlap with the routing signal. The learnable-affine clause in §4.1 separates the normalizers among our backbones, so §4.1, Appendix H and Proposition 1 state one criterion.

**2. The NLinear control: the confound is real, and the result holds.**

We agree on both facts, including that our anchor is the simplified single-Linear variant rather than DLinear's trend-seasonal form, and we built it: a from-scratch NLinear under that anchor's protocol (Linear(512→96), 49K, same optimizer, epochs, batch), differing only by the level anchor, n=10. Our anchor reproduces the published values on all six (ETTh1 0.4187 against 0.419±0.005), as does Residual-IA+.

The effect is real. Across nine datasets at H=96, NLinear beats DLinear on three, all level-drifting: Exchange (−28.9%), ETTh2 (−3.8%), ETTm2 (−7.9%). Elsewhere DLinear is stronger on four and the anchors sit within 0.2% on ETTm1 and Weather, so the substitution cuts both ways.

MOMENT-small, H=96, n=10 per arm, Welch two-sided against the stronger anchor:

| Dataset | Residual-IA+ | DLinear | NLinear | Stronger | Gap | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ETTh1 | 0.4288 | 0.4187 | 0.4289 | DLinear | +2.4% | 0.008 |
| ETTh2 | 0.3456 | 0.3519 | 0.3385 | NLinear | +2.1% | 0.173 |
| ETTm1 | 0.3259 | 0.3259 | 0.3255 | NLinear | +0.1% | 0.923 |
| ETTm2 | 0.1880 | 0.2109 | 0.1943 | NLinear | −3.2% | 0.075 |
| Weather | 0.1967 | 0.2070 | 0.2068 | NLinear | −4.9% | 0.001 |
| Electricity | 0.1564 | 0.1590 | 0.1627 | DLinear | −1.6% | 0.004 |

Residual-IA+ matches or beats the stronger anchor on four of six, mean gap −0.9%. ETTh1 is the only significant loss; ETTh2 does not reach significance.

The margin holds where level anchoring is inert: on Electricity and Weather above, and on Solar, which the recipe never saw, where the anchors differ by 0.3% and Residual-IA+ wins all 20 cells at n=10 (−8.7% at H=96, −11.2% at H=192). On Exchange we agree: the −26.3% over the single-Linear anchor is level anchoring, and against NLinear the cell is parity at H=96 and behind at H=192; we will report it as parity. On the backbone, the reviewer is right that this comparison cannot separate it from the raw branch; App. P.3 takes that up and reports it as dataset-dependent.

The revision will score against both anchors, lead with the count against the stronger, name the anchor accurately wherever it appears, including Figure P.1's caption, which calls the raw branch DLinear-equivalent, and move the anchor comparison and backbone analysis into the main text.

Both concerns focus on the accuracy claim rather than the diagnostic contribution because our presentation put it in front: we led with "5/6 match-or-beat" and titled the appendix "Closing the DLinear Gap". The reviewer read the paper as we wrote it. That said, we would respectfully ask that the paper also be weighed on the diagnostic contribution, which stands as submitted; the title and two of three contributions name it.

Again, we thank the reviewer. We know the effort a reading at this depth takes, and both points have made the paper more accurate. If the reviewer finds them met, we would truly appreciate a reassessment of the score.

content.text:
**What I meant:** an uncorrected p-value is the *permissive* one — it makes things easier to call significant. So when a reviewer complains about missing multiple-comparison correction, the usual suspicion is that uncorrected p-values were used to inflate the authors' wins.

Here it runs the other way. Correcting over the six cells wouldn't cost you a single win: Weather (0.001) and Electricity (0.004) survive Bonferroni and Holm comfortably. The only cell it would touch is ETTh1 at 0.008, right at the 0.0083 threshold — and ETTh1 is your loss. Correcting would let you say "the ETTh1 loss is marginal once corrected"; you don't say that, you say "ETTh1 is the only significant loss." So the uncorrected choice is the one that's harder on you, which is why a "you didn't correct" challenge has no purchase on this table.

**Yes, it's postable.** Everything is checked: all six rows and every gap, mean and p recomputed from the archived per-seed JSONs; the nine-dataset, Solar and Exchange claims verified; all six paper cross-references confirmed against the submitted manuscript (with N.2 now named as Moirai-MoE); the statistics consistent with what you told 8b2Z; 4992 characters, under the 5000 limit. Post it.

I thank the authors for the detailed rebuttal and the new experiments. The minor issues (router parameter count, α initialization, Figure 2, line 64) are resolved However, two substantive issues remain (W3 and W4), and in both cases the rebuttal contradicts either the paper itself or leaves the decisive control missing. My reasons are as follows.

1. The rebuttal's explanation of the Moirai gains contradicts the paper itself
The paper, §4.1 (lines 188–190), states that non-learnable I/O scaling "preserves the (M, Σ) statistics in the hidden states the router reads". This is the stated reason regime (ii) is not vulnerable. The rebuttal's response to my W3 asserts the opposite: Moirai's non-learnable normalization "also strips per-window location-scale from the hidden states, and the raw input lets the router recover it." The rebuttal presents the reversal as "a sharper claim, not a weaker one" without acknowledging that it rewrites the paper's stated mechanism. Table N.2's caption meanwhile hedges in the original direction ("hidden states retain enough signal to avoid collapse"), and the rule offered to Reviewer 8b2Z ("a normalizer causes collapse when it strips routing-relevant statistics at the router's input") silently replaces the paper's learnable-affine criterion.

Which claim is correct?

2. "Residual-IA+ matches or beats DLinear" is confounded by NLinear vs. a simplified DLinear
Two facts from the submission itself: Residual-IA+'s shared raw branch is NLinear (App. P.1, fix (v): y = Linear(x − x_T) + x_T), while the calibration anchor is the simplified single-Linear DLinear without trend-seasonal decomposition (App. A, lines 640–643). NLinear's from-scratch advantage over DLinear on level-drifting data is a known result from [17] itself, and the paper's own Batch-4 analysis (lines 1309–1315) shows the same pattern inside the adapter: the NLinear branch helps most on precisely the non-stationary ETT datasets, "matching NLinear's design rationale."

The headline defense of W1/W4 (65 significant wins vs. 11 losses) therefore compares a method whose base predictor is a stronger linear model against a weaker linear anchor. As reported, the grid cannot distinguish "the backbone adds value" from "NLinear beats a simplified DLinear." The [NEW] Exchange result (a ~10× RR-MoA deficit in Table N.4 flipping to 2/3 match-or-beat) is exactly what level anchoring predicts on near-random-walk data, backbone or not. Add a variant from-scratch NLinear, trained under the same protocol as the DLinear anchor would be persuasive.

""" yet ? Shall we go post now ?

content.text:
Yes. Mapping their comment onto the reply:

**Point 1**
- *"Which claim is correct?"* — answered in the section header and first sentence: the paper's, and it holds in §4.1, N.2's caption and App. H.
- *The contradicting W3 sentence* — withdrawn outright, with the reasoning shown.
- *"without acknowledging that it rewrites the paper's stated mechanism"* — this is answered in substance by naming exactly what the rewrite was: the sentence "described what normalization does to its input, but phrased it as a claim about the encoder's representation." That is their §4.1-vs-rebuttal contradiction, stated in your own words.
- *N.2's caption "hedges in the original direction"* — the reply promotes that caption from hedge to the operative explanation, so the two-regime reading now comes from the paper's own text rather than from a rewrite. This is what defuses the charge.
- *The 8b2Z rule "silently replaces the learnable-affine criterion"* — answered: it's shorthand for App. H's criterion, and §4.1's learnable-affine clause is what separates your backbones, so the three state one criterion.

**Point 2**
- *Both facts* — agreed explicitly, including that your anchor is the simplified single-Linear variant.
- *"Add a variant from-scratch NLinear, trained under the same protocol"* — that is exactly what was built and reported, every cell, n=10.
- *NLinear's known advantage on level-drifting data* — confirmed, not resisted (Exchange −28.9, ETTh2 −3.8, ETTm2 −7.9), with the fact that it cuts both ways.
- *Exchange as level anchoring* — conceded, reclassified as parity.
- *"the grid cannot distinguish the backbone from NLinear-beats-DLinear"* — conceded in as many words.

Two things to be clear-eyed about, neither of which should hold the post:

1. **The full 6×6×4 grid has not been rescored against NLinear.** You deliver MOMENT-small H=96 plus Solar and Exchange, and promise the rescore in the revision. That's the honest scope and it's stated in the table header. The cross-backbone n=3 anchors in your "do not volunteer" file are the answer if they push.
2. **Their Batch-4 citation (lines 1309–1315) goes unanswered** — correctly, since it's evidence for a claim you concede.

Post it.

**Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We thank the reviewer for reading the paper, its appendices and our rebuttal so closely. We believe it takes a great deal of time and effort to do that. We apologise for the slight delay: we wanted the requested control finished first. On the first we stand corrected; on the second we report every cell below.

**1. Which claim is correct: the paper's.**

The paper's claim is correct and holds throughout: §4.1, Table N.2's caption and Appendix H agree. One sentence in our W3 answer described what normalization does to its input, but phrased it as a claim about the encoder's representation. We withdraw it, and want to give visibility into how we got there. Our initial reasoning was that raw input helps Moirai's router for the reason it does on MOMENT, where RevIN removes the statistics and raw routing restores them. That reasoning does not transfer.

Only that clause fails. The diagnosis predicts collapse wherever routing-relevant statistics are stripped from what the router reads. Moirai's routing stays healthy, so those statistics do reach its router, and the gain has the source Table N.2's caption already states: raw-signal routing is information-richer than hidden-state routing even when the hidden states retain enough signal to avoid collapse. The two regimes are therefore collapse-repair where the statistics are stripped, and a richer router input where they are not. This is not App. P.3's Pure Raw-MLP effect: in RR-MoA the raw signal reaches only the router, and the 12–29% figure is RR-MoA against best fixed (Table N.1).

The rule we gave Reviewer 8b2Z is shorthand for the paper's criterion, stated in Appendix H: whether normalization triggers or prevents collapse depends on whether the stripped statistics overlap with the routing signal. The learnable-affine clause in §4.1 separates the normalizers among our backbones, so §4.1, Appendix H and Proposition 1 state one criterion.

**2. The NLinear control: the confound is real, and the result holds.**

We agree on both facts, including that our anchor is the simplified single-Linear variant rather than DLinear's trend-seasonal form, and we built it: a from-scratch NLinear under that anchor's protocol (Linear(512→96), 49K, same optimizer, epochs, batch), differing only by the level anchor, n=10. Our anchor reproduces the published values on all six (ETTh1 0.4187 against 0.419±0.005), as does Residual-IA+.

The effect is real. Across nine datasets at H=96, NLinear beats DLinear on three, all level-drifting: Exchange (−28.9%), ETTh2 (−3.8%), ETTm2 (−7.9%). Elsewhere DLinear is stronger on four and the anchors sit within 0.2% on ETTm1 and Weather, so the substitution cuts both ways.

MOMENT-small, H=96, n=10 per arm, Welch two-sided against the stronger anchor:

| Dataset | Residual-IA+ | DLinear | NLinear | Stronger | Gap | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ETTh1 | 0.4288 | 0.4187 | 0.4289 | DLinear | +2.4% | 0.008 |
| ETTh2 | 0.3456 | 0.3519 | 0.3385 | NLinear | +2.1% | 0.173 |
| ETTm1 | 0.3259 | 0.3259 | 0.3255 | NLinear | +0.1% | 0.923 |
| ETTm2 | 0.1880 | 0.2109 | 0.1943 | NLinear | −3.2% | 0.075 |
| Weather | 0.1967 | 0.2070 | 0.2068 | NLinear | −4.9% | 0.001 |
| Electricity | 0.1564 | 0.1590 | 0.1627 | DLinear | −1.6% | 0.004 |

Residual-IA+ matches or beats the stronger anchor on four of six, mean gap −0.9%. ETTh1 is the only significant loss; ETTh2 does not reach significance.

The margin holds where level anchoring is inert: on Electricity and Weather above, and on Solar, which the recipe never saw, where the anchors differ by 0.3% and Residual-IA+ wins all 20 cells at n=10 (−8.7% at H=96, −11.2% at H=192). On Exchange we agree: the −26.3% over the single-Linear anchor is level anchoring, and against NLinear the cell is parity at H=96 and behind at H=192; we will report it as parity. On the backbone, the reviewer is right that this comparison cannot separate it from the raw branch; App. P.3 takes that up and reports it as dataset-dependent.

The revision will score against both anchors, lead with the count against the stronger, name the anchor accurately wherever it appears, including Figure P.1's caption, which calls the raw branch DLinear-equivalent, and move the anchor comparison and backbone analysis into the main text.

To be explicit: the confusion here comes from our writing, not the reviewer's reading. Both concerns focus on the accuracy claim rather than the diagnostic contribution because our presentation put it in front: we led with "5/6 match-or-beat" and titled the appendix "Closing the DLinear Gap". The reviewer read the paper as we wrote it. That said, we would respectfully ask that the paper also be weighed on the diagnostic contribution, which stands as submitted; the title and two of three contributions name it.

Again, we thank the reviewer. We know the effort a reading at this depth takes, and both points have made the paper more accurate. If the reviewer finds them met, we would truly appreciate a reassessment of the score.

**Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We thank the reviewer for reading the paper, its appendices and our rebuttal so closely. We believe it takes a great deal of time and effort to do that. We apologise for the slight delay: we wanted the requested control finished first. On the first we stand corrected; on the second we report every cell below.

**1. Which claim is correct: the paper's.**

The paper's claim is correct and holds throughout: §4.1, Table N.2's caption and Appendix H agree. One sentence in our W3 answer described what normalization does to its input, but phrased it as a claim about the encoder's representation. We withdraw it, and want to give visibility into how we got there. Our initial reasoning was that raw input helps Moirai's router for the reason it does on MOMENT, where RevIN removes the statistics and raw routing restores them. That reasoning does not transfer.

Only that clause fails. The diagnosis predicts collapse wherever routing-relevant statistics are stripped from what the router reads. Moirai's routing stays healthy, so those statistics do reach its router, and the gain has the source Table N.2's caption already states: raw-signal routing is information-richer than hidden-state routing even when the hidden states retain enough signal to avoid collapse. The two regimes are therefore collapse-repair where the statistics are stripped, and a richer router input where they are not. This is not App. P.3's Pure Raw-MLP effect: in RR-MoA the raw signal reaches only the router, and the 12–29% figure is RR-MoA against best fixed (Table N.1).

The rule we gave Reviewer 8b2Z is shorthand for the paper's criterion, stated in Appendix H: whether normalization triggers or prevents collapse depends on whether the stripped statistics overlap with the routing signal. The learnable-affine clause in §4.1 separates the normalizers among our backbones, so §4.1, Appendix H and Proposition 1 state one criterion.

**2. The NLinear control: the confound is real, and the result holds.**

We agree on both facts, including that our anchor is the simplified single-Linear variant rather than DLinear's trend-seasonal form, and we built it: a from-scratch NLinear under that anchor's protocol (Linear(512→96), 49K, same optimizer, epochs, batch), differing only by the level anchor, n=10. Our anchor reproduces the published values on all six (ETTh1 0.4187 against 0.419±0.005), as does Residual-IA+.

The effect is real. Across nine datasets at H=96, NLinear beats DLinear on three, all level-drifting: Exchange (−28.9%), ETTh2 (−3.8%), ETTm2 (−7.9%). Elsewhere DLinear is stronger on four and the anchors sit within 0.2% on ETTm1 and Weather, so the substitution cuts both ways.

MOMENT-small, H=96, n=10 per arm, Welch two-sided against the stronger anchor:

| Dataset | Residual-IA+ | DLinear | NLinear | Stronger | Gap | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ETTh1 | 0.4288 | 0.4187 | 0.4289 | DLinear | +2.4% | 0.008 |
| ETTh2 | 0.3456 | 0.3519 | 0.3385 | NLinear | +2.1% | 0.173 |
| ETTm1 | 0.3259 | 0.3259 | 0.3255 | NLinear | +0.1% | 0.923 |
| ETTm2 | 0.1880 | 0.2109 | 0.1943 | NLinear | −3.2% | 0.075 |
| Weather | 0.1967 | 0.2070 | 0.2068 | NLinear | −4.9% | 0.001 |
| Electricity | 0.1564 | 0.1590 | 0.1627 | DLinear | −1.6% | 0.004 |

Residual-IA+ matches or beats the stronger anchor on four of six, mean gap −0.9%. ETTh1 is the only significant loss; ETTh2 does not reach significance.

The margin holds where level anchoring is inert: on Electricity and Weather above, and on Solar, which the recipe never saw, where the anchors differ by 0.3% and Residual-IA+ wins all 20 cells at n=10 (−8.7% at H=96, −11.2% at H=192). On Exchange we agree: the −26.3% over the single-Linear anchor is level anchoring, and against NLinear the cell is parity at H=96 and behind at H=192; we will report it as parity. On the backbone, the reviewer is right that this comparison cannot separate it from the raw branch; App. P.3 takes that up and reports it as dataset-dependent.

The revision will score against both anchors, lead with the count against the stronger, name the anchor accurately wherever it appears, including Figure P.1's caption, which calls the raw branch DLinear-equivalent, and move the anchor comparison and backbone analysis into the main text.

To be explicit: the confusion here comes from our writing, not the reviewer's reading. Both concerns focus on the accuracy claim rather than the diagnostic contribution because our presentation put it in front: we led with "5/6 match-or-beat" and titled the appendix "Closing the DLinear Gap". The reviewer read the paper as we wrote it. That said, we would respectfully ask that the paper also be weighed on the diagnostic contribution, which stands as submitted; the title and two of three contributions name it.

Again, we thank the reviewer. We know the effort a reading at this depth takes, and both points have made the paper more accurate. If the reviewer finds them met, we would truly appreciate a reassessment of the score.

**Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We thank the reviewer for reading the paper, its appendices and our rebuttal so closely. We believe it takes a great deal of time and effort to arrive at that feedback. We apologise for the slight delay: we wanted the requested control finished first. On the first we stand corrected; on the second we report every cell below.

**1. Which claim is correct: the paper's.**

The paper's claim is correct throughout: §4.1, Table N.2's caption and Appendix H agree. One sentence in our W3 answer described what normalization does to its input, but phrased it as a claim about the encoder's representation. We withdraw it, and want to give visibility into how we got there. Our initial reasoning was that raw input helps Moirai's router for the reason it does on MOMENT, where RevIN removes the statistics and raw routing restores them. That reasoning does not transfer.

Only that clause fails. The diagnosis predicts collapse wherever routing-relevant statistics are stripped from what the router reads. Moirai's routing stays healthy, so those statistics do reach its router, and the gain has the source Table N.2's caption (Moirai-MoE) states: raw-signal routing is information-richer than hidden-state routing even when the hidden states retain enough signal to avoid collapse. The two regimes are therefore collapse-repair where the statistics are stripped, and a richer router input where they are not. This is not App. P.3's Pure Raw-MLP effect: in RR-MoA the raw signal reaches only the router, and the 12–29% figure is RR-MoA against best fixed (Table N.1).

The rule we gave Reviewer 8b2Z is shorthand for the paper's criterion, stated in Appendix H: whether normalization triggers or prevents collapse depends on whether the stripped statistics overlap with the routing signal. The learnable-affine clause in §4.1 separates the normalizers among our backbones, so §4.1, Appendix H and Proposition 1 state one criterion.

**2. The NLinear control: the confound is real, and the result holds.**

We agree on both facts, including that our anchor is the simplified single-Linear variant rather than DLinear's trend-seasonal form, and we built it: a from-scratch NLinear under that anchor's protocol (Linear(512→96), 49K, same optimizer, epochs, batch), differing only by the level anchor, n=10. Our anchor reproduces the published values on all six (ETTh1 0.4187 against 0.419±0.005), as does Residual-IA+.

The effect is real. Across nine datasets at H=96, NLinear beats DLinear on three, all level-drifting: Exchange (−28.9%), ETTh2 (−3.8%), ETTm2 (−7.9%). Elsewhere DLinear is stronger on four and the anchors sit within 0.2% on ETTm1 and Weather, so the substitution cuts both ways.

MOMENT-small, H=96, n=10 per arm, Welch two-sided against the stronger anchor:

| Dataset | Residual-IA+ | DLinear | NLinear | Stronger | Gap | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ETTh1 | 0.4288 | 0.4187 | 0.4289 | DLinear | +2.4% | 0.008 |
| ETTh2 | 0.3456 | 0.3519 | 0.3385 | NLinear | +2.1% | 0.173 |
| ETTm1 | 0.3259 | 0.3259 | 0.3255 | NLinear | +0.1% | 0.923 |
| ETTm2 | 0.1880 | 0.2109 | 0.1943 | NLinear | −3.2% | 0.075 |
| Weather | 0.1967 | 0.2070 | 0.2068 | NLinear | −4.9% | 0.001 |
| Electricity | 0.1564 | 0.1590 | 0.1627 | DLinear | −1.6% | 0.004 |

Residual-IA+ matches or beats the stronger anchor on four of six, mean gap −0.9%. ETTh1 is the only significant loss; ETTh2 does not reach significance.

The margin holds where level anchoring is inert: on Electricity and Weather above, and on Solar, which the recipe never saw, where the anchors differ by 0.3% and Residual-IA+ wins all 20 cells at n=10 (−8.7% at H=96, −11.2% at H=192). On Exchange we agree: the −26.3% over the single-Linear anchor is level anchoring, and against NLinear the cell is parity at H=96 and behind at H=192; we will report it as parity. On the backbone, the reviewer is right that this comparison cannot separate it from the raw branch; App. P.3 takes that up and reports it as dataset-dependent.

The revision will score against both anchors, lead with the count against the stronger, name the anchor accurately wherever it appears, and move the anchor comparison and backbone analysis into the main text.

To be explicit: the confusion here comes from our writing, not the reviewer's reading. Both concerns focus on the accuracy claim rather than the diagnostic contribution because our presentation put it in front: we led with "5/6 match-or-beat" and titled the appendix "Closing the DLinear Gap". The reviewer read the paper as we wrote it. That said, we would respectfully ask that the paper also be weighed on the diagnostic contribution, which stands as submitted; the title and two of three contributions name it.

Again, we thank the reviewer. We know the effort a reading at this depth takes, and both points have made the paper more accurate. If the reviewer finds them met, we would truly appreciate a reassessment of the score.
